records.title: Change in Tandem
records.text:
Change in Tandem
How inputs and outputs vary together: functions, increasing and decreasing behavior, concavity, and zeros.
A function tells you how an output responds as an input changes. Describing that response, whether it rises or falls and whether it speeds up or slows down, is the foundation for everything else in this course.
Whenever two quantities are linked, a natural question is what one does when the other changes. Functions answer that question precisely. The rest of this unit, from rates of change to polynomial and rational behavior, builds on describing how an output and an input change in tandem.

records.title: Change in Tandem
records.heading: A function gives each input exactly one output.
records.text:
A function gives each input exactly one output.
Each input has exactly one output, but different inputs are allowed to share an output.
A function assigns to each allowed input exactly one output. The set of allowed inputs is the domain, and the set of outputs that actually occur is the range. Two functions are the same function only when they have the same domain and give the same output for every input in it.
A function can appear as a table of values, a graph, an equation, or a verbal description. The representation changes, but the function does not. Moving between representations is a skill you will use in every unit.

records.text:
Increasing and decreasing describe how outputs respond to larger inputs.
Name the interval and the direction. One function can increase in one place and decrease in another.
A function is increasing on an interval if larger inputs always give larger outputs there. It is decreasing on an interval if larger inputs always give smaller outputs there. On a graph read from left to right, rising means increasing and falling means decreasing.
Many functions change direction. A ball thrown upward gains height while it rises and loses height while it falls, so its height function is increasing on one interval and decreasing on the next. Always name the interval when you describe the behavior.

records.text:
Concavity describes how the rate of change is itself changing.
Concave up means the rate of change is increasing. Concave down means the rate of change is decreasing.
Two functions can both be increasing and still look very different. One climbs faster and faster, while the other climbs more and more slowly. Concavity captures that difference. A graph is concave up where its rate of change is increasing, and concave down where its rate of change is decreasing.

records.heading: Zeros are the inputs that make the output zero.
records.text:
Zeros are the inputs that make the output zero.
A zero is an input, not an output. It is the x-value where f(x) = 0.
A zero of a function is an input whose output is 0. On a graph, a real zero is a point where the graph meets the x-axis, so real zeros are also called x-intercepts. If p(x) = (x − 2)(x + 5), then p(2) = 0 and p(−5) = 0, so 2 and −5 are the zeros of p.
From a rule, set the output equal to 0 and solve.
From a table, look for rows whose output is 0.
From a graph, look for x-intercepts.
From a context, ask when the quantity being measured equals 0, such as when a height reaches the ground.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.text:
Rates of Change
Average rates of change over intervals, estimating the rate at a point, and what the sign of a rate tells you.
An average rate of change summarizes how fast an output changes over an interval. Shrinking the interval around a point gives an estimate of how fast the output is changing at that point.
Topic 1.1 described whether outputs rise or fall and whether the rise speeds up or slows down. This topic puts numbers on those ideas. Rates of change are the central tool of the whole course, and they are what makes calculus possible later on.
records.excerpt: Average rates of change over intervals, estimating the rate at a point, and what the sign of a rate tells you.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.heading: The average rate of change compares output change to input change.
records.text:
The average rate of change compares output change to input change.
Average rate of change is change in output divided by change in input, and it belongs to a specific interval.
Over the interval from x = a to x = b, the average rate of change of f is (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). It is the single constant rate that would produce the same overall change in output across the same change in input. Its units are output units per input unit, such as meters per second.
Position of a cyclist, s(t) = t² + 5t

From t = 2 to t = 5 the position changes by 50 − 14 = 36 meters in 3 seconds, so the average rate of change is 36/3 = 12 meters per second. From t = 5 to t = 9 it is (126 − 50)/4 = 19 meters per second. The two answers differ because an average rate depends on the interval, so always state the interval.

records.heading: Small intervals give an estimate of the rate at a point.
records.text:
Small intervals give an estimate of the rate at a point.
To estimate a rate at a point, use the average rate over a small interval at or around that point.
The average over three seconds says little about how fast the cyclist is moving at exactly t = 3. To estimate that, shrink the interval so it starts or surrounds t = 3. The average rate of change over a very small interval approximates the rate of change at the point, whenever the function has a rate of change there.

records.heading: Compare rates at two points using small intervals near each.
records.text:
Compare rates at two points using small intervals near each.
Compare rates at two points by estimating each with a small interval, then comparing the numbers.
To decide where an output changes faster, estimate the rate near each input and compare the results. Near t = 3 the cyclist's rate is about 11 meters per second. Using the interval from 7.9 to 8.1 seconds, the average rate is (106.11 − 101.91)/0.2 = 21 meters per second. The cyclist is changing position faster near t = 8 than near t = 3.
Use small intervals of similar width around each point. A wide interval blends together many different rates and can hide which point is really changing faster.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.heading: The sign of a rate tells you how the two quantities move together.
records.text:
The sign of a rate tells you how the two quantities move together.
A rate has a sign, a size, and units. Say all three when you interpret it.
A positive rate means the two quantities move in the same direction: as the input increases, the output increases.
A negative rate means they move in opposite directions: as the input increases, the output decreases.
A rate close to zero means the output is changing very little compared with the input.
State every rate with its meaning and its units. A good sentence has the form: at about this input, the output is increasing or decreasing at about this many output units per input unit. For example, the average rate of −0.5 degrees per minute for cooling coffee says the temperature is falling by half a degree each minute on average.

records.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
records.text:
Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
How average rates behave for linear and quadratic functions, secant slopes, and reading concavity from changing rates.
The pattern of average rates over equal-width intervals reveals the type of function. Constant rates mean a linear function, and rates that change by a constant amount are the signature of a quadratic function.
Topic 1.2 gave you a way to calculate and interpret rates. This topic studies how those rates themselves behave. Looking at the rate of change of the rates is the first step toward recognizing function families from their data.
records.excerpt: How average rates behave for linear and quadratic functions, secant slopes, and reading concavity from changing rates.

records.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
records.heading: A linear function has the same average rate of change everywhere.
records.text:
A linear function has the same average rate of change everywhere.
Constant average rates mean linear. The rate of change of those rates is zero.
A linear function f(x) = mx + b changes by the same amount m for every one-unit step in x. Its average rate of change is the constant m over every interval of any width. The graph is a line, and the line has no concavity because its rate never changes.

A sequence is a function whose inputs are the positive integers, so it lists outputs in order. When consecutive terms differ by the same amount, the average rate of change from one term to the next is constant, and the sequence behaves like a linear function. Because the average rates of a linear function never change, they change at a rate of zero.

A secant line is a line through two points on a graph. Its slope is rise over run, which is exactly the change in output divided by the change in input. So the average rate of change of f on [a, b] equals the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)).
For f(x) = x², the secant line through (1, 1) and (3, 9) has slope (9 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 4. That number is also the average rate of change of f on [1, 3]. Picturing the secant line is a useful way to see why average rates are different on different intervals: different intervals produce secant lines with different slopes.

records.text:
Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
Polynomial vocabulary, local and global extrema, how zeros and turning points relate, and inflection points.
A polynomial's graph is shaped by how its rate of change rises and falls. Extrema mark where it changes direction, and inflection points mark where it changes concavity.
You have studied how outputs change and how rates themselves change. Polynomial functions are the first large family where both ideas appear in rich combination, and they are built from the simple power functions you already know.

Degree comes from the highest power of x after the polynomial is fully expanded.

Extrema occur where a function switches between increasing and decreasing.
A local extremum is the best output nearby. A global extremum is the best output everywhere.
A local maximum occurs where a function switches from increasing to decreasing, and a local minimum occurs where it switches from decreasing to increasing. A local extremum can also occur at an included endpoint of the domain. A local extremum whose output beats every other output of the function is a global maximum or a global minimum.

records.text:
Between two real zeros, a polynomial must turn around.
At least one turning point sits between any two distinct real zeros of a polynomial.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
Zeros and factors, multiplicity, conjugate pairs of non-real zeros, finding degree from differences, and even and odd symmetry.
A polynomial's zeros, with their multiplicities, are its fingerprints. They determine its factors, where its graph crosses or touches the x-axis, and how many complex zeros it has.
Topic 1.4 showed that zeros and turning points are linked. Here zeros take center stage. You will work with real zeros that appear as x-intercepts and with non-real zeros that never appear on the graph but still count toward the degree.
records.excerpt: Zeros and factors, multiplicity, conjugate pairs of non-real zeros, finding degree from differences, and even and odd symmetry.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.heading: A real zero corresponds to a linear factor.
records.text:
A real zero corresponds to a linear factor.
Zeros give factors, x-intercepts, and the boundaries of the intervals where a polynomial is positive or negative.
A number a is a zero of a polynomial p when p(a) = 0. For a real number a, the expression (x − a) is a factor of p exactly when a is a zero. Real zeros are also the x-intercepts of the graph. For example, p(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 factors as (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3), so its zeros are 1, −2, and 3.
Real zeros also split the number line into intervals where the polynomial keeps one sign. To solve p(x) > 0, find the zeros, then test one input in each interval between them.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.heading: Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
records.text:
Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
Non-real zeros pair up as conjugates, so they can reduce the number of x-intercepts without changing the degree.
A complex number has the form a + bi, where a and b are real and i² = −1. When a polynomial has real coefficients, its non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs: if a + bi is a zero with b ≠ 0, then a − bi is a zero too. For instance, x² + 4 has zeros 2i and −2i, and x² − 2x + 5 has zeros 1 + 2i and 1 − 2i.
Non-real zeros never appear as x-intercepts, but they still count toward the degree. Because they come in pairs, a real-coefficient polynomial of odd degree always has at least one real zero. The polynomial (x² + 4)(x − 1) has degree 3 and three complex zeros, 2i, −2i, and 1, but its graph meets the x-axis only once.

Even and odd functions have symmetry.
Replace x with −x. The same function means even, the opposite means odd, and anything else means neither.
A function f is an even function if f(−x) = f(x) for every x in its domain. Its graph is symmetric about the y-axis, and power functions with even exponents, such as x² and x⁴, are even. A function f is an odd function if f(−x) = −f(x). Its graph is symmetric about the origin, and power functions with odd exponents, such as x and x³, are odd.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
Limit notation, why the leading term controls the far left and far right of the graph, and the four end-behavior cases.
Far from the origin, a polynomial behaves like its leading term. Whether the degree is even or odd and whether the leading coefficient is positive or negative gives all four possible end behaviors.
Zeros and turning points describe the middle of a polynomial's graph. End behavior describes the two far edges. Together they let you sketch a believable graph without plotting many points.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
records.heading: End behavior asks what happens as inputs grow without bound.
records.text:
End behavior asks what happens as inputs grow without bound.
Limit notation says in symbols what the outputs do at the far left and far right.
End behavior describes the outputs of a function when the input moves far to the right (x increases without bound, written x → ∞) or far to the left (x decreases without bound, written x → −∞). Limit notation records the result. The statement lim x→∞ f(x) = ∞ says that as x increases without bound, the outputs also increase without bound.
Likewise lim x→−∞ f(x) = −∞ says that as x decreases without bound, the outputs decrease without bound, which means they become more and more negative. The symbols ∞ and −∞ describe a direction of growth, not a number the function ever reaches.

records.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
records.text:
Rational Functions and End Behavior
What a rational function is, and how comparing leading terms gives horizontal and slant asymptotes.
For large inputs, a rational function behaves like the quotient of its leading terms. Comparing the sizes of the numerator and denominator tells you whether the outputs settle near a number, follow a line, or grow without bound.
Polynomial end behavior came from one leading term. A rational function has two polynomials fighting for control, so the question becomes which one grows faster, or whether they grow at the same pace.
records.excerpt: What a rational function is, and how comparing leading terms gives horizontal and slant asymptotes.

records.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
records.heading: A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials.
records.text:
A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials.
A rational function is a polynomial divided by a polynomial, and it is undefined where the denominator is zero.
A rational function can be written r(x) = p(x)/q(x), where p and q are polynomials and q is not the zero polynomial. At each input, the output measures the size of the numerator relative to the size of the denominator. The function is undefined wherever q(x) = 0.

records.title: Rational Functions and Zeros
records.text:
Rational Functions and Zeros
Finding the zeros of a rational function and using signs to decide where it is positive or negative.
A rational function can change sign only at a zero of the numerator or at an input where the denominator is zero. Finding those inputs splits the number line into intervals where the sign stays the same.
A quotient is zero only when the numerator is zero and the quotient exists. That gives a short checklist for locating zeros, and the same inputs mark the boundaries between positive and negative stretches.

records.title: Rational Functions and Zeros
records.heading: A zero of a rational function is a zero of the numerator that is not excluded by the denominator.
records.text:
A zero of a rational function is a zero of the numerator that is not excluded by the denominator.
Set the numerator equal to 0, then throw out any solution that also makes the denominator 0.
A fraction equals 0 only when its numerator equals 0 and the fraction is defined. So the zeros of the rational function r(x) = p(x)/q(x) are the zeros of p(x) at which q(x) is not 0. For r(x) = (x − 2)(x + 3)/(x − 1), the zeros are x = 2 and x = −3. The input x = 1 makes the denominator zero, so r(1) does not exist.
For r(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1), the numerator is zero at both x = 1 and x = −1. But r(1) is undefined, so x = 1 is not a zero. The only zero is x = −1. Topic 1.10 explains what the graph does at x = 1.

records.text:
Rational Functions and Vertical Asymptotes
Where the denominator is zero but the numerator is not, and how one-sided limits describe the graph nearby.
Near an input that makes the denominator zero but not the numerator, the outputs become very large in size. A sign chart tells you whether they head toward ∞ or −∞ on each side.

records.text:
A vertical asymptote sits where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not.

records.title: Rational Functions and Holes
records.text:
Rational Functions and Holes
When a factor cancels, the graph has a hole instead of an asymptote, and how to find its coordinates.
A rational function can be undefined at an input without having an asymptote there. When a factor of the denominator cancels completely, the graph approaches a single point and has a hole at that input.
In Topic 1.9, every zero of the denominator led to an asymptote because the numerator was not zero there. This topic covers the other case, in which the numerator is zero at the same input.
records.excerpt: When a factor cancels, the graph has a hole instead of an asymptote, and how to find its coordinates.

records.title: Rational Functions and Holes
records.heading: A hole appears when a factor cancels out of the denominator.
records.text:
A hole appears when a factor cancels out of the denominator.
Cancel common factors. If no factor of (x − a) is left in the denominator, there is a hole at x = a.
Suppose the factor (x − a) appears in both the numerator and the denominator of a rational function. The function is undefined at x = a, because the original denominator is 0 there. But after the common factor is cancelled, nothing in the denominator is zero at x = a. The graph approaches a single point and has a hole at x = a.
The multiplicities matter. A hole occurs when the factor appears in the numerator at least as many times as in the denominator. For r(x) = (x − 2)²/(x − 2), cancelling one factor leaves x − 2, so the graph has a hole at x = 2. For r(x) = (x − 2)/(x − 2)², cancelling leaves 1/(x − 2), so x = 2 is a vertical asymptote instead.

records.text:
Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
Rewriting expressions by factoring, expanding, dividing, and using the binomial theorem, and choosing the form that shows what you need.
Equivalent expressions give the same outputs, but each form makes some features easy to see and others hard. Skilled work with functions includes choosing the form that fits the question.
Earlier topics factored expressions to find zeros, holes, and asymptotes, and divided to find a slant asymptote. This topic gathers those moves and adds the binomial theorem for expanding powers.

Each form of an expression shows different features.

Two expressions are equivalent expressions when they have the same value for every input in their shared domain. The polynomial (x − 1)²(x + 2) and the polynomial x³ − 3x + 2 are equivalent. Neither is better in general. The factored form shows the zeros and their multiplicities at once, while the expanded form shows the degree, the leading term, and the value at x = 0.

records.text:
Polynomial long division rewrites a rational function as a quotient plus a remainder.
Divide, write quotient plus remainder over divisor, and check by multiplying back.
Polynomial long division divides a polynomial p(x) by a polynomial d(x) and gives a quotient q(x) and a remainder r(x) with p(x) = d(x)·q(x) + r(x), where r has a lower degree than d. Dividing both sides by d(x) turns this into p(x)/d(x) = q(x) + r(x)/d(x). For a rational function, this divided form is useful because r(x)/d(x) shrinks toward 0 at the ends.
For (x² + 3x + 5)/(x − 1), the first term of the quotient is x, because x·(x − 1) = x² − x. Subtracting leaves 4x + 5, and the next term is 4, since 4·(x − 1) = 4x − 4. The remainder is 9. So x² + 3x + 5 = (x − 1)(x + 4) + 9, and the rational function equals x + 4 + 9/(x − 1).
The quotient x + 4 is the slant asymptote. When the numerator and denominator have the same degree, the quotient is a constant, and that constant is the horizontal asymptote, matching the ratio of leading coefficients from Topic 1.7. You can always check a division by multiplying the divisor and the quotient and adding the remainder.

The binomial theorem expands a power of a sum without repeated multiplying.
Use the row of Pascal's triangle for the coefficients, and carry any coefficient and sign inside a and b.

records.title: Transformations of Functions
records.text:
Transformations of Functions
How shifts, dilations, and reflections change a function's graph, its points, its domain and range, and its asymptotes.
Changing a function's rule in a small way moves or reshapes its graph in a predictable way. Changes to the input act on the horizontal direction, and changes to the output act on the vertical direction.
Every function family in this course is built from a few basic graphs by transformations. Knowing how a change in the rule moves each point lets you describe a new function from one you already understand.
records.excerpt: How shifts, dilations, and reflections change a function's graph, its points, its domain and range, and its asymptotes.

records.title: Transformations of Functions
records.heading: Adding to the input or to the output translates the graph.
records.text:
Adding to the input or to the output translates the graph.
A change inside the parentheses moves the graph sideways in the opposite direction. A change outside moves it up or down.
A translation slides every point of a graph the same distance without changing its shape. Adding a constant to the output, as in g(x) = f(x) + d, moves the graph up by d units (down if d is negative). Adding to the input, as in g(x) = f(x − c), moves the graph right by c units (left if c is negative).
The horizontal direction feels backward at first. For g(x) = f(x − 3), the output g(5) equals f(2), so the point (2, f(2)) of f appears at x = 5. Each point of f moves 3 units to the right.

records.heading: Multiplying the output or input stretches, compresses, or reflects the graph.
records.text:
Multiplying the output or input stretches, compresses, or reflects the graph.
Outside multiplication changes y-values. Inside multiplication changes x-values by the reciprocal.
A dilation stretches or compresses a graph. In g(x) = a·f(x), every output is multiplied by a, so the graph is stretched vertically if |a| > 1 and compressed if |a| < 1. If a is negative, the graph is also reflected across the x-axis. A reflection flips the graph over a line.
In h(x) = f(bx), every input is multiplied by b before f acts, so each point moves to x-coordinate (original x)/b. The graph is compressed horizontally by a factor of 1/|b| when |b| > 1 and stretched when |b| < 1. If b is negative, the graph is reflected across the y-axis.

records.heading: Combined transformations are read one piece at a time.
records.text:
Combined transformations are read one piece at a time.
Move the key points one transformation at a time, inside changes first for x-values and outside changes first for y-values.
Many transformations combine a dilation, a reflection, and a translation. For g(x) = a·f(b(x − h)) + k, the factor b and the shift h act on the inputs, and a and k act on the outputs. A reliable method is to track a few key points of f, such as zeros and extreme points, and move each one.
Let f(x) = x² − 1, which has zeros at x = −1 and x = 1, and let g(x) = 2f(x − 3). The zeros of g occur where x − 3 = −1 or x − 3 = 1, so at x = 2 and x = 4. The vertex of f at (0, −1) moves to (3, −2), because the shift sends 0 to 3 and the dilation doubles −1.

records.text:
Transformations move the asymptotes and change the domain and range.
Apply the same transformation to the asymptotes, the domain, and the range as you apply to the points.
A horizontal translation moves vertical asymptotes by the same amount, and a vertical translation moves horizontal asymptotes. The parent function f(x) = 1/x has the vertical asymptote x = 0 and the horizontal asymptote y = 0. For g(x) = 1/(x − 2) + 3, the asymptotes are x = 2 and y = 3. The domain of g is all real numbers except 2, and its range is all real numbers except 3.
Output changes also change the range. The function f(x) = x² has range [0, ∞). For h(x) = −2f(x) + 3, the values −2x² are at most 0, so h has range (−∞, 3].

records.title: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
records.text:
Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
Choosing a type of function to model a situation, using successive differences, and stating the assumptions and restrictions that come with a model.
A model is a function chosen to describe a situation, and it is only as good as the pattern it matches and the assumptions behind it. Choosing a model means connecting the structure of the data to the structure of a function family, then saying where the model applies.
You now know several function families and how to read rates, zeros, asymptotes, and transformations. This topic asks which family to reach for, and how to be honest about what the model assumes and where it breaks down.

records.title: Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
records.heading: The pattern in the data points to a type of function.
records.text:
The pattern in the data points to a type of function.
Describe how the output changes, then choose the function family whose structure has that same pattern.
A mathematical model is a function that describes how two quantities in a situation are related. Before fitting anything, ask what the situation says about how the output changes. The average rate of change over equal steps is a strong clue.
Clues for choosing a model
What you notice
Model that fits
Equal input steps give equal output changes
Linear function
The changes in output themselves change by a constant amount
Quadratic function
Constant differences appear only at a higher level (third differences, for example)
Polynomial function of higher degree
The output depends on a ratio, such as a fixed total shared among n people, or levels off near a value
Rational function

Successive differences reveal the degree of a polynomial model.
Keep taking differences until they become constant. The number of times you subtracted is the degree.
When the inputs are equally spaced, successive differences are found by subtracting each output from the next, then repeating on the new list. If the nth differences are constant, a polynomial of degree n fits the data. First differences that are constant indicate a linear function, and second differences that are constant indicate a quadratic function.

records.text:
Every model has assumptions and restrictions on its domain and range.
State what the model assumes, restrict the domain and range to what makes sense, and be cautious about extrapolation.
A ball is thrown upward from a height of 5 feet, and its height after t seconds is modeled by h(t) = −16t² + 48t + 5 feet. This model assumes the ball moves only under gravity, with no air resistance and no wind. It also describes only the flight itself: the domain is 0 ≤ t ≤ about 3.1 seconds, when the ball lands. The range is 0 ≤ h ≤ 41 feet, since the greatest height is h(1.5) = 41 and the ball ends at ground level.

records.title: Function Model Construction and Application
records.text:
Function Model Construction and Application
Building a function model from conditions, a parent function, or technology, and interpreting the model in context.
A model is built from conditions: what it must equal at certain inputs, where it is zero, and where it levels off. Once built, its features are not just math facts. Each one answers a question in the situation.
Topic 1.13 chose the type of model. This topic finds the constants that make that type fit, and then reads the finished model back into the situation.

Zeros and a point determine a polynomial model.
Write the form that shows the given features, then use one more condition to find the constant.
If a polynomial has zeros at r₁, r₂, …, it has factors (x − r₁), (x − r₂), …, and an unknown constant multiple a. Use one more point on the graph to find a. Suppose a cubic has zeros at −2, 1, and 3 and passes through (0, 12). Then p(x) = a(x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3). At x = 0 this gives 6a = 12, so a = 2 and p(x) = 2(x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3).

A parent function plus a transformation builds a model.
Use the asymptotes or vertex to set the shifts, then one point to set the scale factor.
A parent function is a basic function, such as x², x³, or 1/x, from which others are made by translations, dilations, and reflections. Start with the parent that has the right shape, then use asymptotes, vertices, or points to choose the transformation.

records.heading: Rational models describe costs and rates shared over a quantity.
records.text:
Rational models describe costs and rates shared over a quantity.
In a rational model, the horizontal asymptote is a long-run value and the vertical asymptote often marks an input outside the situation.
A print shop charges a $120 setup fee plus $3 per poster. The average cost per poster for n posters is A(n) = (120 + 3n)/n, with n a positive whole number. This is a rational function. Its vertical asymptote at n = 0 is outside the domain of the situation, and its horizontal asymptote y = 3 describes the long-run cost.

records.title: Function Model Construction and Application
records.heading: Each feature of a model answers a question in context.
records.text:
Each feature of a model answers a question in context.
Write conclusions in a full sentence with units, and check them against the domain and the assumptions.
A store models its revenue, in dollars, by R(p) = p(80 − 4p) when it sells an item at a price of p dollars. The zeros are p = 0 and p = 20. At p = 0 nothing is earned because the item is free. At p = 20 the factor 80 − 4p is 0, so no one buys and revenue is 0. A quadratic is symmetric, so the maximum occurs halfway between the zeros, at p = 10. There R(10) = 10·40 = 400, so the greatest revenue is $400 at a price of $10.
A complete interpretation names the quantity, the units, and the situation: The store earns its greatest revenue, $400, when it charges $10. Restating only R(10) = 400 leaves the reader to guess what it means. Also keep the answer within the domain, 0 ≤ p ≤ 20, where the revenue is not negative.
